analysis.one_liner: Blocked EPA from issuing stricter soot and smog air standards until current, weaker ones were met.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 42 House members, never received a committee vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the EPA from issuing any new or tighter national air quality standards for particulate matter (fine soot) and ozone (smog) until existing standards were fully met — which for ozone meant waiting until 2010. That would have delayed the tougher pollution limits on power plants, factories, and vehicles that EPA was preparing in 1997. The bill never moved past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Utilities that burn coal, industrial manufacturers, refiners, and other large emitters, because the bill would have postponed for years the compliance costs of tighter soot and smog limits. Supporters argued this protected jobs in areas that had not yet met even the existing standards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal-burning utilities and large industrial polluters

how_it_helps.text: It would have barred any new or revised national ambient air quality standard for particulate matter until after December 31, 2001, and for ozone until after November 15, 2010 — the dates by which existing standards were supposed to be attained [S3].
The CRS summary confirms it prohibited EPA from issuing any new or revised soot or smog standard until the existing standards' attainment deadlines had passed [S2].

This would have shielded emitters from the cost of meeting the stricter fine-particle and ozone limits EPA proposed in late 1996 and finalized in 1997, which were the first-ever standard for fine particulate matter.

analysis.who_pays: People living in areas with dirty air, especially children, the elderly, and people with asthma and heart disease, because stricter limits on fine soot and smog — the pollutants linked to asthma attacks, hospital visits, and premature deaths — would have been delayed for years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents of polluted areas, especially kids and asthmatics

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith case for the bill: many counties were still struggling to meet the existing standards, and supporters argued that piling on new standards before old ones were attained imposed costs that threatened industrial jobs, particularly in the Midwest [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the cost: delaying tighter fine-particle standards postpones documented health benefits, since fine soot is linked to premature deaths and respiratory illness, and the delay ran well past 2001 for soot and to 2010 for smog [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose — sequencing new standards behind existing ones — had surface appeal, but its actual effect was to freeze air pollution rules at 1990s levels for up to a decade while the health science supported tighter limits. The compliance savings for utilities and factories would have come at the price of continued exposure to pollutants tied to asthma and premature death. Weighing that trade, the cost to public health clearly outweighed the scheduling rationale.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, neither of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Ney introduced the Job Protection Act of 1997 in the House on June 11, 1997 [S1].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S5].
On June 18, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The bill drew 42 cosponsors, 39 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the bill still stuck in subcommittee, so it never reached the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who breathe the air: because the bill died, EPA's stricter fine-particle and ozone standards issued in 1997 were not blocked, and the industries the bill would have shielded did not get their delay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People breathing the air; the stricter EPA standards survived

for.name: Rep. Bob Ney
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited 42 cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the Clean Air Act
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill, leaving it in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican — 39 of 42 cosponsors were Republicans, with only 3 Democrats — and the bill went nowhere in a committee chaired by a member of the majority party.

industries.note: Utilities burning coal are among the largest sources of fine particulate matter and ozone precursors; the bill would have postponed for years the standards that require them to cut those emissions, keeping cleanup costs off their books and the pollution in the air.

Industrial facilities face control costs under soot and smog standards, and many counties with heavy industry had not attained the existing standards; the bill's title itself framed the stakes as jobs versus tighter air rules [S3].

Refineries and chemical plants emit both volatile organic compounds and particulates; delaying tighter ozone and fine-particle standards would have delayed the emission controls those facilities would otherwise have had to install.
